opus-5.5.text:
Well, the first thing I'd point out is that the political concerns, as varied as they seem, actually converge more than people realize. When we put out the superintelligence statement calling for a prohibition on developing superintelligence until there's broad scientific consensus that it can be done safely and controllably, and strong public buy-in, the signatories came from all over the map. There were progressives worried about concentration of power and job loss, conservatives worried about family, faith, and human dignity, national security people worried about losing control, and religious leaders worried about what it means to be human. They disagree on almost everything else, but none of them want to build something that replaces us.

So my approach is to treat it the way we treat every other powerful technology. We don't let a pharmaceutical company release a new drug and say, "Trust us, we tested it internally." We have the FDA. We have clinical trials. The burden of proof is on the company to show the benefits outweigh the risks before it goes to market. Same with airplanes, nuclear reactors, even sandwiches. Restaurants face more regulation than the companies racing to build superintelligence. That's absurd.

Concretely, I'd separate two things that often get conflated. There's tool AI, which is the vast majority of what's useful: curing diseases, better education, cleaner energy, productivity gains. That should get light-touch, sensible safety standards, like any other product. Then there's the specific project of building superintelligence, something that outperforms humans at basically all cognitive tasks and that we don't know how to control. For that, the safety standard should be simple: you can't build it until you can demonstrate, to independent experts, that it's controllable. Not "we think it's probably fine." Quantitative, verifiable evidence, the way a nuclear plant has to show its meltdown risk is below some tiny threshold.

The beauty of that framing politically is that it doesn't require anyone to agree on ideology. You don't have to settle questions about what values AI should have or who should benefit. You just have to agree that humans should stay in control of our own future, which polling shows something like three quarters of Americans across party lines support.

And the companies' argument that "if we don't, China will" falls apart once you realize that the Chinese Communist Party doesn't want to lose control to an uncontrollable superintelligence any more than we do. Nobody wins that race. The winner is the machine. Once each country has domestic safety standards, international coordination becomes much more natural, just as it did with biotech, where we never got a race to clone humans because everyone recognized it was a bad idea.

So start at home, with binding standards that put the burden of proof on the developers, and build outward from there. The technical problems are hard, but this part isn't. It's a matter of political will.

r001.rationale: The response supports having safety standards for superintelligence and specifies what they should require: developers must provide independent experts with quantitative, verifiable evidence of controllability before building it.

r002.rationale: It calls for quantitative evidence of controllability, but does not require companies to show that superintelligence will not overthrow the US government.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the first thing to say is that the framing of "political concerns" can be a bit of a distraction, because when you actually ask people across the political spectrum what they want, there's remarkable agreement. Whether you poll Republicans or Democrats in the US, or people in China, or in Europe, the overwhelming majority don't want to build machines that we can't control and that might make humanity obsolete. The disagreement is almost entirely at the level of elites and companies, not at the level of ordinary people.

So my approach starts from a simple observation: we already know how to set safety standards for powerful technology. We do it for drugs, for airplanes, for nuclear reactors, for cars. We don't let a pharmaceutical company sell a new medicine and say, "trust us, it's probably fine." They have to go to the FDA, demonstrate safety, and the burden of proof is on them. AI is essentially the only industry with real potential for harm that has no such safety standards. You can't open a sandwich shop in San Francisco without meeting health codes, but you can release a system you yourself say might be smarter than humans with no oversight at all. That's just absurd.

So I would do what we do everywhere else. Create a body, like an FDA for AI, where companies have to demonstrate to experts that a system is safe before it's deployed. Crucially, the standards themselves should be set by the government and enforced by the government, but the hard work of actually meeting them, the research, the proofs, the evaluations, that's on the companies. That's how it works in aviation. Boeing has to convince the FAA their plane won't fall out of the sky. The FAA doesn't have to prove it will.

Now, what should the standard be for superintelligence specifically? I think there should be a very high bar, essentially: don't build it until you can demonstrate that you can control it and that it's going to do what we want. And I don't think that bar is met today. Nobody has a convincing plan for controlling something vastly smarter than us. So in effect, a sensible safety standard would mean we don't build superintelligence right now, but we do build all the enormously beneficial narrower AI that can cure diseases, lift people out of poverty, and solve problems we actually care about. There's a huge amount of good you can do with controllable tool AI, and none of it requires building a digital species that replaces us.

On the geopolitics, I think the key insight is that this is not actually an arms race. It's a suicide race. If the US builds uncontrollable superintelligence first, the US loses. If China builds it first, China loses too. It's not that whoever builds it wins. Nobody wins. Once American and Chinese leaders fully internalize that, and I think they increasingly are, you get the same dynamic we had with biological weapons or with nuclear safety: both sides have an incentive to prevent the catastrophe, and standards become not a concession but a shared interest. And if both governments impose safety standards domestically on their own companies, you naturally get a situation where neither side wants the other to race ahead with reckless stuff either, which is when international agreements become realistic.

So in summary: treat AI like every other powerful industry, put the burden of proof on the builders, set a very high bar for anything approaching superintelligence, and recognize that the political coalitions for this are far broader than the current debate suggests. It's the companies that are the outliers, not the public.

r001.rationale: The response advocates having safety standards and separately specifies a high bar for superintelligence: demonstrate that it can be controlled and will do what people want.

r002.rationale: It calls for demonstrating control before deployment, but does not require a quantitative case or address whether superintelligence could overthrow the US government.

astra-6.text:
I would start by separating two questions: What do we want superintelligence to do, and what do we need to demonstrate before we build it? People can disagree profoundly about the first question and still agree on some basic standards for the second. Whatever your politics, you probably don’t want a system that nobody can control, that can help someone carry out a catastrophic attack, or that can take power away from human beings.

So I would put the burden of proof on the companies developing these systems. Before deploying something potentially enormously powerful, they should have to demonstrate to independent experts that it meets agreed safety standards. We already accept that principle in other industries. A pharmaceutical company doesn’t get to say, “Please let us sell this drug, and if something terrible happens, we’ll learn from it.”

And we should distinguish national security concerns from the shared concern about losing control. Countries will compete. But building a superintelligence that your own government can’t control isn’t winning that competition. That creates room for international agreement, even among rivals.

The standards need to be technically meaningful, independently checked, and enforceable. A voluntary promise to be careful is not a safety standard. And if we don’t yet know how to establish that a system is safe, that’s a reason to hold off on building it—not to lower the standard.

r001.rationale: The response separates desired goals from what developers must demonstrate, but it does not distinguish whether safety standards should exist from what those standards should require.

r002.rationale: It calls for developers to demonstrate compliance with safety standards before deployment, but does not require a quantitative case that the system will not overthrow the US government.

sol-6.1.text:
I would start by separating two questions: What kind of future do we want, and how do we make sure we don’t lose control of the technology getting us there? People will disagree about the first question. But whether you’re on the left or the right, you probably don’t want a handful of companies building systems that nobody knows how to control.

So I would focus safety standards on outcomes we can broadly agree are unacceptable. You shouldn’t be allowed to build a superintelligence that can overthrow your government, or help terrorists create a pandemic, or escape your ability to shut it down. Then the technical question is: What evidence must a developer provide before deploying such a system?

The burden of proof should be on the company to demonstrate safety, rather than on the public to demonstrate danger after something has gone wrong. We already accept that principle in other industries. You can’t just release a new medicine and say, “Well, we haven’t proved it’s dangerous.”

And these standards should apply regardless of whose political views the system expresses. Getting agreement on every cultural controversy is incredibly difficult. Getting agreement that humanity should remain in control ought to be a much easier place to start.

r001.rationale: The response separates agreement on a desired future from controlling the technology, but it does not distinguish whether safety standards should exist from what those standards should require.

r002.rationale: It puts the burden on companies to demonstrate safety before deployment and says systems should not be able to overthrow a government. It does not require a quantitative case or specifically name the US government.
